name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
role: Genevan philosopher of popular sovereignty and the general will (1712-1778)
summary: Rousseau held that legitimate authority rests only on the consent of citizens who make the laws themselves as a sovereign people, with government a subordinate agent and representation of sovereignty rejected. He favoured small republics of modest equality and civic virtue, a civil religion, public education and citizen militias, and condemned luxury, hereditary rule and the corrupting effects of the arts and sciences. He also held that women should be subordinate to men within the family and excluded from public life.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Poland chapter XII says the State must not remain without defenders and relies on a militia, and says a state that disbands its army invites attack.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He calls hereditary aristocracy the worst of governments (III.5), yet in Poland leaves the nobility in place as the one hereditary body.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The Arts and Sciences discourse treats progress in sciences and arts as a source of corruption, so he opposes speeding it up.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The Second Discourse preface says animals, being sentient, should partake of natural right and not be wantonly ill-treated.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: II.3 says the general will needs that there be no partial societies in the State, though he says nothing on a leader to bypass them.

character-from-environment.rationale: Poland chapter II says national institutions shape the genius, character, tastes and manners of a people, and Emile builds on education forming the person.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: Social Contract I.4 says war is between States and gives a right to kill defenders only while they bear arms, and no right to take the lives of those who surrender.

clerical-rule.rationale: IV.8 says wherever the clergy is a corporate body it is master and legislator, an evil that makes good polity impossible.

conscription.rationale: Poland chapter XII holds that each citizen should be a soldier by duty, none by profession, and Social Contract II.5 says the citizen must die when the State requires it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: IV.2 states that no one can be made subject without his consent and I.4 denies any natural authority of one man over another.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The Discourse on the Arts and Sciences and Social Contract III.4 condemn luxury as corrupting both rich and poor, and the Poland text builds its reforms on making luxury and money contemptible.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Political Economy and Poland favour exempting necessaries such as corn and rice from taxation and putting duties on luxuries.

death-penalty.rationale: Social Contract II.5 defends executing malefactors as public enemies, while saying the State has no right to kill anyone it can leave alive without danger.

decide-locally.rationale: He prefers small states (II.9), urges a federal structure of small administrations for Poland, and wants no capital in a larger State (III.13).

democracy-becomes-oligarchy.rationale: III.4 says that when government functions are shared the less numerous body sooner or later acquires the greatest authority.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: IV.2 says long debates, dissensions and tumult proclaim the ascendancy of particular interests and the decline of the State.

direct-votes.rationale: III.15 says every law the people has not ratified in person is null and void, and that sovereignty cannot be represented.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Emile V says the inequality of the sexes' duties is of reason, not prejudice, and that women should not complain of man-made laws.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: In I.3 he answers that all power comes from God by saying so does all sickness, and grounds authority in the social compact (I.6) instead.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Social Contract II.4 says every service a citizen can render he must render when the Sovereign demands it, after the total alienation of I.6.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Social Contract III.6 condemns hereditary crowns as risking children and imbeciles as rulers, and in Poland he urges that a king's sons be excluded from the throne.

elective-rulers.rationale: Social Contract III.5 calls elective aristocracy the best form, and in Poland he defends the elective crown against heredity, saying heredity in the crown and freedom in the nation are incompatible.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Social Contract IV.6 allows the laws to be silenced under a dictator in the greatest danger to the State, for a brief fixed term only, and with no power to make laws.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Poland tells the Poles to account alliances and treaties as things of no moment, since states honour them only from interest.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: SEP reports that Rousseau rejects individuals insisting on rights as a check on the sovereign; rights are specified by the sovereign.

equal-outcomes.rationale: He wants limits so that none is rich enough to buy another or poor enough to sell himself, but states that equality does not mean identical wealth or power (Social Contract II.11).

experts-over-public.rationale: He gives the wisest the executive (III.5) yet reserves all lawmaking to the whole people (III.15), so the evidence is split.

flat-income-tax.rationale: He argues that taxes should rise with property and that superfluities, not necessaries, be taxed, which is the opposite of an equal percentage on all (Political Economy).

free-public-college.rationale: He wants a free public education system for Poland, or at least fees the poor can afford with free scholarships (chapter IV), though he speaks of schools generally, not universities.

free-trade.rationale: He approvingly quotes d'Argenson that foreign commerce enriches individuals but not the nation, and proposes duties on imported luxuries (Political Economy, Poland).

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: I.7 and II.11 present the social compact as guarantee against all personal dependence, which he calls force taken from the State.

freedom-is-self-government-of-desire.rationale: Social Contract I.8 says moral liberty alone makes man truly master of himself, for the impulse of appetite is slavery and obedience to a self-prescribed law is liberty.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Emile V says the sexes' moral differences follow the law of nature, and that perfect man and woman should no more be alike in mind than in face.

gradual-change.rationale: Poland I and VI advise a foreigner against rash change, and warn against freeing serfs before making them fit for liberty, so reform proceeds step by step.

harm-principle.rationale: The sovereign is sole judge of what the community needs to control (II.4), and he allows censors, a civil religion and public education to shape conduct, beyond preventing harm.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Poland chapter IV wants the child to read of his own land, know its provinces at twelve and its history at fifteen.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Social Contract I.9 accepts first occupancy of unowned land only on conditions: no one lives there, only what is needed is taken, and labour and cultivation mark possession.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: The Discourses portray the early state of nature and simple early societies as happier, with inequality, arts and refinement bringing decline.

land-use-tenure.rationale: I.9 subordinates holdings to the community's right and limits first occupancy to need and labour, but he never says that land is held only while used; Political Economy also stresses families keeping goods.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Laws derive from the general will in the Social Contract, and Emile's Savoyard Vicar rejects scripture and revelation as the guide.

local-production.rationale: He tells Poland to multiply domestic production and consumption of foodstuffs and quotes d'Argenson that foreign commerce gains the nation nothing (Social Contract II.11 note).

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Poland chapter II urges honorific privileges and memorials keeping alive the memory of those who served and died for the country.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The Discourse on the Arts and Sciences says arts and letters fling garlands of flowers over men's chains and make them love their slavery.

minority-veto.rationale: IV.2 says apart from the original contract the majority always binds the rest, and Poland calls the liberum veto an instrument of oppression to be curbed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: III.6 ranks monarchy below republican government and condemns hereditary succession, while accepting it as a form compatible with law in large States.

national-self-determination.rationale: Social Contract III.13 says no one nation can legitimately be made subject to another, since the essence of the body politic is freedom.

natural-rulers.rationale: III.5 calls it the best and most natural arrangement that the wisest should govern the many, in elective aristocracy.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: IV.3 says lot suits democracy and judicial posts but that real democracy is an ideal; talents-based posts such as military ones should be chosen, so he gives a mixed answer.

participatory-democracy.rationale: III.15 and III.12-14 require the sovereign people to assemble regularly in person, and say a State is lost when citizens say 'what does it matter to me?'

patriotic-education.rationale: Poland chapter IV wants every Pole educated in national history, laws and heroes so that at twenty he is a Pole and not another sort of man.

people-in-arms.rationale: Poland chapter XII replaces regular troops with a militia in which every inhabitant is a soldier when necessary, and says only standing armies let the executive enslave a state.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: Emile (Book III) holds that every member of society must work and that manual labour is the occupation nearest to the state of nature, so even the rich should learn a trade.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: IV.2 treats near-unanimity as the sign of a healthy body politic, yet states that the majority vote binds all outside the original compact.

positive-liberty.rationale: II.11 says liberty cannot exist without equality and that none may be poor enough to be forced to sell himself.

premarital-sex.rationale: Emile V requires that the woman be chaste and keep her reputation, and treats her unfaithfulness as treason.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Poland chapters II-III say national institutions shape a people's character and tastes and that no Pole should be able to become a Russian.

priority-to-poor.rationale: He calls protecting the poor against the tyranny of the rich the most necessary and difficult task of government (Political Economy), though he prefers preventing poverty to relief.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: II.4 and II.6 hold that law is general in object and application and that the sovereign cannot decree on particular persons or facts.

property-fundamental.rationale: Political Economy calls property the most sacred civil right, yet the Social Contract (I.9) makes every individual's right subordinate to the community's claim over all goods; his own texts point both ways.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Social Contract I.9 holds that each owner's right is always subordinate to the community's right over all, owners being depositaries of the public good.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Emile's creed makes conscience and sentiment a guide to God and duty alongside reason, which he says alone cannot supply it.

recall-officials.rationale: Social Contract III.18 provides periodic assemblies asking whether the people wishes to keep the form of government and its officers, and Poland ties deputies to their constituents.

rehabilitation.rationale: II.5 says there is no ill-doer who could not be turned to some good and that frequent punishments show weakness in government.

religion-illusion.rationale: IV.8 says no State has ever been founded without a religious basis, and Emile defends God and the immortal soul against materialism.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Discourse on Inequality says the popular insurrection deposing a despot is as lawful as his acts, and III.18 lets the people recall government.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The Second Discourse says the earth belongs to nobody and its fruits to all, yet the Social Contract recognises limited property; he gives no compensation scheme.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Emile (Book I) says the more men are massed in cities the more corrupt they become, and Social Contract III.13 pictures towns built from the ruins of countryside houses.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Social Contract I.3 rejects 'all power comes from God' as grounds for obedience, comparing it to sickness, and denies any natural or divine right of rulers.

school-vouchers.rationale: Political Economy calls public education under state regulations and magistrates a fundamental rule of legitimate government, and Poland sets the law to regulate studies, against parental choice of school.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: The Vicar in Emile says revelations degrade God and breed intolerance, rejecting scriptural authority.

separate-church-state.rationale: Social Contract IV.8 blames the division between theological and political power for making good polity impossible and prescribes a civil religion fixed by the Sovereign.

separated-powers.rationale: He separates legislative and executive and values the tribunate as a check (III.4, IV.5), but holds sovereignty indivisible and rejects dividing it among powers (II.2).

shared-human-nature.rationale: Social Contract I.2 derives common liberty from the nature of man, and the Second Discourse founds natural right on the shared compassion and self-preservation of humans.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Emile V states that nature gave the husband superiority and a wife owes obedience, and that she follows her husband's religion.

simple-living.rationale: He praises simple manners and home-spun labour over courtly refinement (Arts and Sciences) and tells the Poles to limit luxury, though self-sufficiency as such is not his theme.

single-common-good.rationale: II.3 and II.4 make the general will aim at the common interest alone and warn that factions and particular interests destroy it.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Social Contract treats the prince as a minister bound by law, and Poland binds the king by law and the pacta conventa.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The Vicar's creed in Emile holds man free and moved by an immaterial substance.

state-harmful.rationale: Social Contract I.6 holds that the social compact is necessary because the state of nature can no longer subsist, so the State is indispensable.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: IV.8 requires citizens to profess a civil religion including the existence of a mighty and beneficent Divinity.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: IV.7 gives censors the task of preserving public morality and Poland designs games and national institutions to shape habits.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In the Discourse on Political Economy he argues that those holding superfluities should be taxed on everything above necessaries, and that luxury duties ease the poor and burden the rich to check inequality.

taxation-theft.rationale: Political Economy says members must contribute from their property to the State and that taxes are legitimate when the people consents; he rejects the idea of taxation as theft.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The First Discourse argues that the advance of arts and sciences corrupted morals rather than improving them.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Poland chapter XII says anyone who wants to be free ought not to want to be a conqueror and Poland should renounce all hope of conquest.

traditional-family.rationale: Emile V calls the preservation of a united family a labour of love without which the race would perish, and stresses the wife's duties to it.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Poland chapter IV wants youth trained together in public games and exercises of the nation, with military drills, though not 'uniformed movements' as such.

universal-morality.rationale: The Savoyard Vicar in Emile holds conscience an innate universal judge of good and evil and sets natural religion above the diversity of revelations.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Social Contract II.11 and its note say the extremes of rich and poor are fatal to the common good, because between them public liberty is put up to auction, the one buying and the other selling.

widespread-small-property.rationale: He urges allowing neither rich men nor beggars (Social Contract II.11, note) and tells Poland to have neither beggars nor millionaires, with labour on a modest holding the basis of ownership (I.9).

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: III.15 says that as soon as any man says 'what does it matter to me' of public affairs the State is lost.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Emile V assigns women a distinct moral nature (care of children, modesty, gentleness), as against men's strength and activity.

women-suffrage.rationale: SEP states that Rousseau's citizens are exclusively male and women have no voice in the general will; Emile subordinates women to men.

notes: Researched themes: government and elections, sovereignty and representation, property and taxation, religion and civil religion, war and the military, nationhood and education, women and family, technology and progress. Not answered: health, welfare, drugs, sexuality, immigration, modern finance and environment, where the sources give no stated position. Sources are Rousseau's own texts read in the Project Gutenberg editions (via the local mirror), the Poland text and the SEP. Letter to d'Alembert and the Corsican Constitutional Project were not read. Poland (1772) is advice for a specific country and is treated as his words on politics, not a general doctrine.
